links.note: Verse 60 calls good children (நன்மக்கட் பேறு) the ornament of a home's excellence. Verse 61 raises the same பேறு to the top of everything one can gain and specifies the children as அறிவறிந்த, those who know what should be known. Read together, the chapter on children opens by taking up the last word of the chapter on the wife and narrowing 'good' to 'knowing'.

Verse 61 says that among all things gained (பெறுமவற்றுள்) 'we' know of nothing to set beside knowing children. Verse 162 says that among excellent gains (விழுப்பேற்றின்) nothing equals (அஃதொப்பது இல்லை) being free of envy. The two top rankings conflict only if each superlative is read literally as a ranking across all gains; read as each chapter's idiom of praise they do not.

Both verses rank their subject first by the author's own witness in the first person plural: 61 has யாமறிவது இல்லை ('we know of none') for knowing children, 300 has யாமெய்யாக் கண்டவற்றுள் இல்லை ('among what we have seen as true there is none') for truthfulness. The pairing shows the same rare device, the poet's 'we', used to vouch for a household good and for a virtue of speech.

Verse 62 says evils will not touch a person in all seven births (எழுபிறப்பும் தீயவை தீண்டா) if they get children of character who bring no blame. Verse 398 says the learning gained in one birth is a protection in seven (எழுமையும் ஏமாப்புடைத்து). Both name a good of this life whose protection outlasts it by seven births: in one case one's children, in the other one's own learning.

Verse 62 has blameless children keep evil away through seven births (எழுபிறப்பும்). Verse 835 has the fool, in one birth's doing (ஒருமைச் செயல்), make the mire (அளறு) he sinks in for seven (எழுமையும்). The same seven-birth reckoning is applied in the opposite direction, once to a safeguard and once to a ruin made by oneself.

Verse 44 says that if a household life fears blame (பழியஞ்சி) and shares its food, its line (வழி) never fails. Verse 62 says that if one gets children in whom blame does not grow (பழிபிறங்கா), no evil touches one for seven births. In 44 the parent's freedom from blame secures the descendants; in 62 the descendants' freedom from blame secures the parent.

Verse 63 says people call their children their wealth (தம்பொருள் என்ப தம் மக்கள்), and ties that wealth to deeds (வினையான் வரும்). Verse 114 says whether people are worthy or not is seen from their எச்சம், what they leave behind, which Parimelazhagar takes as their offspring and Kalaignar as the name they leave. On Parimelazhagar's reading the pair makes children both a person's property and the evidence by which that person is judged.

Verse 63 reports the saying that one's children are one's wealth (தம்பொருள்). Verse 400 says learning is the imperishable wealth (கேடில் விழுச்செல்வம்) and that other things are not wealth (மாடல்ல). Both move the word for property from goods to something else, but 400 denies the title to everything other than learning, while 63 only reports what people say.

Verse 64 says the gruel (கூழ்) stirred by one's children's small hands is far sweeter than amrita. Verse 1065 says that though it is gruel thin as clear water (தெண்ணீர் அடுபுற்கை), nothing is sweeter than eating what one's own effort brought (தாள் தந்தது). In both the plainest food is the sweetest because of whose hands stand behind it, the child's in one and one's own labour in the other.

Verse 64 ranks gruel handled by one's children above amrita (அமிழ்தினும் ஆற்ற இனிதே). Verse 82 says that even the medicine of deathlessness (சாவா மருந்து) is not to be wanted if eaten alone while a guest stays outside. Both use the divine food as the measure and then place a household relation above it, the child at the meal in 64 and the guest at the door in 82.

Verse 64 sets a child's messy gruel above amrita. In 1103 the lover asks whether the world of the lotus-eyed one (தாமரைக் கண்ணான் உலகு) can be sweeter (இனிதுகொல்) than sleeping on the soft arms of the one he loves; Parimelazhagar has him say this to a companion who reproved him. The same move, a heavenly standard of sweetness outdone by an intimate bodily one, appears in the parent's voice in Book 1 and in a lover's speech in Book 3.

Verse 65 names two sense pleasures a child gives: touching the child's body is joy to the body (உடற்கின்பம்) and hearing its words is joy to the ear (இன்பம் செவிக்கு). In 1101 the lover says the five senses, seeing, hearing, tasting, smelling and touching (கண்டுகேட்டு உண்டுயிர்த்து உற்றறியும்), all have their objects in one woman. Both list pleasures sense by sense and locate them in a single loved person, a child in one and a lover in the other.

Verse 66 says only those who have not heard their own children's prattle call the flute (குழல்) and the lute sweet. In 1228 the woman left alone says the herdsman's flute (ஆயன் குழல்) is now a messenger of the burning evening and a weapon that kills; Parimelazhagar notes that it had been sweet to her before. In both the flute stands for accepted sweetness, and in both that sweetness is made to depend on the hearer's situation.

Verse 67 states what a father does for a son (தந்தை மகற்காற்றும் நன்றி): he makes him sit at the front of the assembly. Verse 70 states the son's help in return (மகன் தந்தைக்கு ஆற்றும் உதவி): that people ask what penance his father did to get him. The two are built as a matching pair, and the son's return is paid in public speech, in the same assembly where the father placed him.

Verse 67 makes it the father's gift that the son sits ahead in the assembly (அவையத்து முந்தி இருப்ப). Verse 715 says the best of good things is the restraint of not speaking first among elders (முதுவருள் முந்து கிளவாச் செறிவு). The shared root முந்து shows the limit: standing first in the assembly is the goal, but being first to speak before one's seniors is what the book warns against.

Verse 67 says a father's good to his son is to make him sit foremost in the assembly; Parimelazhagar takes this as making him learned beyond the learned there. Verse 722 says those called learned among the learned (கற்றாருள் கற்றார்) are those who can make what they learned go home before the learned. 722 supplies what the front seat of 67 requires in practice: learning that can be delivered in front of that assembly.

Verse 68 says one's children's understanding (அறிவுடைமை) is sweet to all beings on the great earth (மன்னுயிர்க்கெல்லாம் இனிது); Parimelazhagar reads தம்மின் as 'more than to oneself', while Kalaignar and Subramuniyaswami take it as children who surpass their parents. Verse 399 says the learned love learning more on seeing that what delights them delights the world (தாமின்புறுவது உலகின்புறக் கண்டு). Both treat knowledge as a pleasure that is not private: the parent's pride in 68 and the scholar's delight in 399 are each measured against the world's share in it.

Verse 69 says a mother rejoices more than at the hour of birth when she hears her son called சான்றோன். Verse 923 says drunken joy is painful even before the mother who bore one (ஈன்றாள் முகத்தேயும் இன்னாது), and asks what it must then be before the சான்றோர். Both verses set the mother beside the worthy as the two audiences of a son's conduct; 923 shows that her gladness in 69 is not unconditional, though Parimelazhagar calls her one who is pleased whatever he does.

Verse 69 has the mother's joy grow when she hears others call her son worthy (சான்றோன் எனக் கேட்ட தாய்). Verse 1047 says one in poverty unconnected with virtue (அறஞ்சாரா நல்குரவு) is looked on as a stranger even by the mother who bore him (ஈன்ற தாயானும் பிறன்போல நோக்கப்படும்). In both the mother's regard follows the son's standing, rising with his name in 69 and withdrawn in 1047.

Verse 69 says what gladdens a mother most is hearing her son called சான்றோன். Verse 656 says that even if one must see one's mother hungry (ஈன்றாள் பசி காண்பான் ஆயினும்), one should not do the deed the சான்றோர் condemn. Read with 69, the rule of 656 does not set the mother against the worthy: the judgment of the worthy that 656 obeys is the judgment the mother of 69 most wants to hear.

Verse 70 defines the son's help to his father as the saying 'what penance did this one's father do?' (இவன் தந்தை என்நோற்றான் கொல்). Verse 67 defines the father's good to the son as making him sit foremost in the assembly. The pair closes a circle: the father's gift is the son's standing, and the son's gift is the credit that standing reflects back on the father.

Verse 70 has onlookers explain a good son by asking what the father did as penance (என்நோற்றான்). Verse 265 says தவம் is striven for here because whatever is wanted is obtained as wanted (வேண்டிய வேண்டியாங்கு எய்தலால்). The onlookers' question in 70 assumes the doctrine 265 states, and it applies that doctrine to a son.

Verse 71 asks whether there is any bolt that shuts love in (அன்பிற்கும் உண்டோ அடைக்குந்தாழ்), since the tears of the loving give it away. In 1251 the woman says the axe of desire breaks the door of restraint that is fastened with the bolt of shame (நாணுத்தாழ் வீழ்த்த கதவு). The same figure of a bolt that cannot hold is used for household affection (அன்பு) in Book 1 and for a lover's desire (காமம்) in Book 3.

Verse 71 says the small tears (புன்கணீர்) of the loving proclaim their love; Parimelazhagar specifies tears shed at the suffering of those they love. Verse 828 says a weapon lies hidden in an enemy's worshipping hands, and that the tears an enemy has wept are the same (ஒன்னார் அழுத கண்ணீரும் அனைத்து). Tears are evidence of love in 71 only when they come from the loving; 828 warns that tears as such prove nothing.

Verse 71 says tears raise a public noise (பூசல் தரும்) about the love inside. In 1180 the woman says it is not hard for the town to get at the secret (மறை) of those like her whose eyes are beaten drums (அறைபறை கண்ணார்). In both the eyes make public what the heart holds, and both describe this as sound: a clamour in 71, a drum in 1180.

Verse 72 says the loveless belong to themselves in everything (எல்லாம் தமக்குரியர்) while the loving belong to others (பிறர்க்கு) even in their bones. Verse 1009 says wealth piled up by putting love aside (அன்பொரீஇ), denying oneself and ignoring virtue will be taken by others (கொள்வார் பிறர்). 1009 gives the outcome of the stance in 72: what the loveless keep for themselves ends with பிறர் anyway.

Verse 72 says those who have love belong to others even in their bones (என்பும் உரியர் பிறர்க்கு). Verse 220 says that if ruin comes through ஒப்புரவு, that ruin is worth buying even by selling oneself (விற்றுக்கோள் தக்கது). Both carry giving past one's goods to one's own person, 72 as a description of love and 220 as the price of duty to the community.

Verse 73 says the tie of the life with the body (ஆருயிர்க்கு என்போடு இயைந்த தொடர்பு) is, they say, a matter of being joined with love (அன்போடு இயைந்த வழக்கு); Parimelazhagar takes embodiment as the result of a course meant for joining with love. In 1122 the lover says the bond between him and the woman is what the bond between body and life is (உடம்பொடு உயிரிடை என்ன). 73 explains the union of body and life by love, and the lover in 1122 measures his love by that union.

Verse 73 treats the joining of life and body (என்போடு இயைந்த தொடர்பு) as something fitted to love. Verse 338 says the friendship between body and life (உடம்பொடு உயிரிடை நட்பு) is like a bird flying off and leaving its குடம்பை alone. The pairing sets a limit on 73: the bond that exists for love's sake is, in the chapter on impermanence, one the life will abandon.

Verse 73 says the life's connection with the bone (என்போடு) goes with love. Verse 80 says the seat of life (உயிர்நிலை) follows love, and that for those without it the body is bone wrapped in skin (என்புதோல் போர்த்த உடம்பு). The chapter's last verse gives the negative of 73: take away the love and what remains of the union is the bone alone.

Verse 74 says love gives birth (ஈனும்) to eagerness, and that gives birth to friendship, an unsought distinction (நாடாச் சிறப்பு). Verse 757 calls அருள் the child born of love (அன்பீன் குழவி), raised by the foster-mother wealth. Both use the figure of birth for what comes out of அன்பு, and together they give love two offspring, friendship in the home and grace toward all.

Verse 74 derives friendship (நண்பு) from love by way of eagerness (ஆர்வம்) and calls it a distinction that is not sought (நாடா). Verse 785 says meeting and long acquaintance are not needed, because feeling itself (உணர்ச்சிதான்) gives the claim of friendship. The friendship chapter of Book 2 keeps the account given in Book 1: friendship comes from an inner disposition and not from arrangement or contact.

Verse 45 says that if household life has love and virtue (அன்பும் அறனும்), that is its character and its fruit (பண்பும் பயனும்). Verse 75 says the distinction reached by those who have had joy in the world (வையகத்து இன்புற்றார் எய்தும் சிறப்பு) is, they say, the result of a life settled in love (அன்புற்று அமர்ந்த வழக்கு); Parimelazhagar reads the distinction as heaven after household joy. 75 spells out the 'fruit' that 45 only names, and credits it to love.

Verse 39 says only what comes through virtue is joy (அறத்தான் வருவதே இன்பம்) and everything else lies outside it. Verse 75 traces the joy and distinction people reach in the world to a life settled in love (அன்புற்று அமர்ந்த வழக்கு). Set side by side, 75 adds love to the source that 39 confines to அறம், which agrees with verse 45's coupling of the two.

Verse 76 says the ignorant hold that love supports only virtue, while it is the help (துணை) for மறம் as well; Kalaignar reads மறம் as valour, Parimelazhagar as the hostility that love removes. Verse 862 asks how a man without love (அன்பிலன்), without allies and without strength of his own can wear down an enemy's might. On Kalaignar's reading 862 is the case in point: in Book 2 love is listed first among the things a fighter needs.

Verse 76 says love is the ally not only of virtue but of மறம்; the link holds on the reading, Kalaignar's, that மறம் is valour. Verse 773 says fierceness is called great manhood (பேராண்மை), and that helping a foe in trouble (ஊராண்மை) is its cutting edge (எஃகு). Both refuse to keep kindness and martial courage in separate compartments.

Verse 77 says அறம் scorches what has no love as the sun scorches what has no bones (வெயில்போலக் காயுமே). Verse 204 says that if one plots another's ruin, அறம் plots the plotter's ruin (அறஞ்சூழும் சூழ்ந்தவன் கேடு). In both அறம் is an agent that acts against a person, and Parimelazhagar glosses it in both places as அறக்கடவுள், the god of virtue.

Verse 77 has அறம் burn the loveless. Verse 130 has அறம் watch for its moment (செவ்வி அறம்பார்க்கும்) and enter by the path to the one who has guarded against anger and learned restraint. The two show the same personified virtue in both directions: it seeks out the self-governed and dries up the loveless.

Verse 77 compares the loveless to a thing without bones (என்பிலது) dried by the sun; Kalaignar and Subramuniyaswami take it as a worm. Verse 80 says the body of those without love is bones wrapped in skin (என்புதோல் போர்த்த உடம்பு). The chapter uses bone twice for the loveless in opposite ways, once as what they lack and once as all they are.

Verse 78 says a life with no love within is like a dried tree putting out shoots on hard ground (வற்றல் மரம் தளிர்த்தற்று), which Parimelazhagar takes as something that does not happen. In 1106 the lover says her touch makes his life sprout each time they meet (உறுதோறு உயிர் தளிர்ப்ப). The verb தளிர் carries both: life sprouts where love is, and 78 uses the same sprouting to mark what a loveless life cannot do.

Verse 78 likens the loveless life to a withered tree on hard ground. Verse 576 says those who have eyes and no kindly regard are like trees fixed in the soil (மண்ணோடியைந்த மரத்தனையர்). In both a person without the inward quality, அன்பு in one and கண்ணோட்டம் in the other, is reduced to a tree, alive in form and without response.

Verse 79 asks what all the outer parts can do (புறத்துறுப்பெல்லாம் எவன்செய்யும்) for those who lack love, the inner part (அகத்துறுப்பு). Verse 574 asks what eyes do (எவன் செய்யும்), beyond seeming to be in the face, when they have no கண்ணோட்டம். The same question in the same words is put to the whole body in 79 and to one organ in 574: a part is judged by the disposition it serves.

Verse 79 says the outer limbs are of no use without the inner limb, love. Verse 407 says the fine looks (எழில்நலம்) of one without subtle, penetrating understanding are like those of a well-made clay doll (மண்மாண் புனைபாவை). Both set a complete exterior against a missing interior, love in Book 1 and understanding in Book 2.

Verse 80 says the seat of life (உயிர்நிலை) goes by way of love (அன்பின் வழியது). Verse 255 says உயிர்நிலை lies in not eating flesh (உண்ணாமை உள்ளது உயிர்நிலை); Parimelazhagar reads this as life's staying in the body resting on that virtue. The rare word உயிர்நிலை is used in both to make a moral quality, love or not eating flesh, the condition of being alive at all.

Verse 80 says that for those without love the body is only bones wrapped in skin (என்புதோல் போர்த்த உடம்பு). Verse 1020 says the movements of those with no shame within (நாண் அகத்தில்லார்) are like a wooden puppet feigning life by its string (மரப்பாவை ... உயிர்மருட்டியற்று). Both describe a moving body that lacks an inward quality as something without life in it, a frame of bone in one and a puppet in the other.
